title: The tomb in Shiraz
hook: people gather at Hafiz's tomb to recite his poems
tomorrow: Zoe writes her own ghazal for tonight. where does her name go?

segments.voice: Yesterday, versions: new poems under an old name. Not Hafiz, said kindly, with the real line ready. Today, the place where the real lines are said out loud.
screen: `NOT HAFIZ.` → `WHERE THE REAL LINES ARE SAID.`

segments.voice: Inés is going to her grandmother's grave for the first time since the burial, and she's asked Zoe to come. In the car she says it plainly: I don't know what you even do there. Yesterday's question had an answer waiting in Shiraz. People go to Hafiz's grave, and they read him his own poems.
screen: `THE FIRST VISIT.` → `WHAT DO YOU EVEN DO THERE?` → `READ HIM HIS OWN POEMS.`

segments.voice: Hafiz saw it coming. In one ghazal he writes: when you pass by my grave, ask for a blessing, for it will become a place of pilgrimage for the free spirits of the world. Today his tomb stands in a garden in Shiraz, the Hafezieh. Visitors recite his ghazals there, some open the Divan for a line, some just sit with a hand on the stone. Under that custom sits a teaching. In Islam, visiting a grave is called ziyarat. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says he had once forbidden visiting graves, but now: visit them. Another hadith there gives the reason: they remind you of death. Hadiths in the same book teach a greeting of peace for the dead, and the Prophet asking forgiveness for them. The question for this week: why go back to a grave at all? Inés's own tradition answers too. The Catholic Bible says, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." Shared: you go back, and you bring words to the one you lost; both traditions pray for the dead. Honestly different: Catholics pray for the soul, trusting that prayer helps it on its way to God. At the Hafezieh, people also bring the poet his own words, the way he asked. Two ways of standing at a grave, neither one a copy of the other.
screen: `A PLACE OF PILGRIMAGE, HE SAID.` · `THE HAFEZIEH: POEMS AT THE STONE.` · `ZIYARAT: THEY REMIND YOU OF DEATH.` · `PRAY FOR THE DEAD.` · then, large: `RECITING AT THE TOMB.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one grave or memorial you know, or one person you've lost. Count three things they gave you, slowly, one for each long breath. If you pray, you can pray for them in the words of your own tradition; if not, simply hold them in mind.
The tomb in Shiraz: Hafiz's grave in a garden, where visitors recite his poems, just as one of his ghazals foresaw.
Your line: reciting at the tomb, bringing their own words back to them. Seven days into Hafiz.
